members.statement: Treat translation as a prototype category with a periphery (adaptation, version, transcreation, localization), and when there is no single stable source text (multilingual versions, unstable, continually updated, or orally transmitted sources) broaden the source-to-target model rather than forcing the traditional configuration.

Decide whether a translation is overt (its source is tied to its culture and time, so it cannot pretend to be an original and seeks second-level functional equivalence at the level of language, register, and genre, letting target receivers eavesdrop) or covert (its source is not culture-bound, so it should read as an original through a cultural filter that adapts cultural elements at the levels of language and register), treat the distinction as a cline, and produce a version rather than a translation when the source genre has no equivalent target form.

Expect the recurring cross-cultural swing between literal and free translation and the systematic losses that rendering into another language incurs (reversed word order, stylistic elevation, omitted repetition, reduced paratext, restructuring), and recognize that a highly literal method that borrows everything tends to fail.

Work the Vinay and Darbelnet procedure ladder: within direct translation use borrowing, calque, or literal translation, prescribing literal rendering as the basis of good translation and sacrificing literalness only for structural or metalinguistic reasons after checking that meaning is preserved, and when a literal rendering is unacceptable on grammatical, syntactic, or pragmatic grounds move to oblique translation through transposition (change of part of speech, the commonest structural change), modulation (change of viewpoint, the touchstone of a good translator, used when a correct rendering is unidiomatic or awkward), equivalence (idiomatic rendering for idioms and proverbs), or adaptation (change of cultural reference when the source situation is absent).

Define a good translation by its effect on the target reader, so completely transfusing the merit of the original that a target reader apprehends and feels it as a source reader does, and pitch it to the target readership's level of education and understanding, which usually differs from the translator's own.

Treat translation as inferential communication, making the target optimally relevant so the receiver derives adequate contextual effects without unnecessary effort by supplying communicative clues, and decide whether and how to communicate the informative intention, whether to translate descriptively or interpretively, and the degree of resemblance to the source from the receiver's cognitive environment, since a translation can fail when it does not match the audience's expectations for form or prestige.

Treat translation as a distinct linguistic genre with its own norms and ends whose value lies in forcing the reader out of native linguistic habits and into the foreign author's world; correspondingly, a translation that reduces the work to transmissible information conveys only the inessential and is, on this view, bad translation.

Treat translation as at once interpretation and creation, involving a choice among the source's possible interpretations and a choice among the target's possible expressions of that meaning, and expect the translator in practice to apply a pessimistic minimax strategy — accepting the solution promising the most effect for the least effort provided its value clears the minimum his standards admit — while recognizing that the importance he assigns a stylistic device is a relative value weighed against competing values such as linguistic purity, that preserving a device is an implicit bet on what fraction of readers will feel the language violated, and that a preserved formal feature communicates only to the subset of readers competent to decode it (Sapphic metre versus apparent free verse), so the likely audience composition must be weighed.

Orient every translation consciously on the domestication-to-foreignization axis, choosing between moving the writer toward the reader (naturalizing) and moving the reader toward the writer (foreignizing), and know which pole you are choosing and why.

Orient a translation on the domestication-foreignization axis, where domestication is an ethnocentric, fluent, invisible reduction of the foreign to receiving values that moves the author toward the reader and dominates Anglo-American culture, and foreignization chooses a foreign text and a non-fluent, estranging method that makes the translator visible and highlights the source's identity by moving the reader toward the author, realizing foreignization through text choice and techniques such as close adherence to structure, calques, archaisms, and heterogeneous discourse, and treating the two as a continuum on an ethical level of values and a discursive level of fluency versus resistancy while noting that foreignization is relative and historically contingent.
Mine translators' prefaces and self-accounts as evidence of the translation method and stance adopted, while allowing for their bias.

Weigh translators' self-accounts as evidence of method and stance while allowing for bias and their intuitive voice-led vocabulary, recognizing that much of the labour behind a translation is invisible and that a translation is a non-neutral critical act whose ideology resides in the translator's voicing, stance, and place of enunciation.

Treat cross-language equivalence as partial and relative rather than identity: because there is no full equivalence between code-units, translate whole messages rather than code-units, and treat translatability as a matter of degree and adequacy, since all cognitive content is conveyable in some form.

Take the message, not the code-unit, as the unit of equivalence: since synonymy is ordinarily not complete equivalence and there is usually no full equivalence between code-units across languages, translation recodes two equivalent messages in two different codes ('equivalence in difference', the cardinal problem of language), which is why comparing languages by their mutual translatability and building differential bilingual dictionaries (intension and extension) and grammars is of high theoretical and practical value.

Reject cross-code identity as the basis of translation: the referential argument fails because a word signifies through its systematic relations within its code, not through the object, the conceptual argument fails for lack of any grammar-cognition correlation, and the universals argument yields only trivial universals; point-by-point identity would turn translation into copying, mimicry, or transliteration because it cannot capture the surrounding code structure (a sentential adverb acceptable in Spanish is despised in written English), and identity is useless because universal grammar is a matter of absolute competence whereas translation is a matter of probabilistic performance — its very interest springing from the structural mismatch of codes, so that where whole structures are identical the recoding is academic and not even worthy of the name translation.

Analyse translation shifts against a system-level baseline, treating a shift as a departure from formal correspondence, of level (grammar in one language, lexis in another) or category (structural, class, unit or rank, or intra-system), and judge equivalence by communicative features such as function, relevance, situation, and culture rather than by formal criteria alone or by idealized invented examples divorced from whole texts.

Analyze departures from formal correspondence as Catford's shifts, of two major types: level shifts, which render a source item at one linguistic level by a target equivalent at another and are possible only between grammar and lexis (Russian perfective aspect, having no marked English counterpart, is rendered lexically by a word such as 'achieve'), and category shifts, which presuppose some formal correspondence and come in four kinds — structure shifts (the most frequent), class shifts, unit or rank shifts, and intra-system shifts — noting that normal unbounded translation sets equivalences at whatever rank fits while rank-bound translation confined below the sentence produces bad translation, and that an intra-system shift (English 'advice' becoming French plural 'des conseils') shows even corresponding systems do not guarantee term-for-term equivalence.

Translate the same source differently according to the target purpose and commission, consciously and consistently by a principle decided for each case, and state the skopos explicitly or implicitly in a commission or brief comprising a goal and its conditions such as deadline and fee, negotiated with the commissioner and with the translator advising on feasibility, letting adequacy override equivalence as the measure.

Make the translation commission an explicit instruction stating both the goal and the conditions for attaining it (including deadline and fee), negotiated with the client — who may hold an imprecise or false picture of how the text will be received, so the translator should offer argued suggestions — while remembering that a commission's realizability depends on the target culture's circumstances, not the source's (too great a discrepancy yields not a translation but at most a rewrite); this relativizes the once-dominant demand to translate 'as literally as possible' into just one legitimate skopos among many, does not require adaptation to target expectations (a deliberately marked translation and every hybrid are equally accommodated), and yields a threefold value: making an often-denied aim explicit, expanding strategy and releasing the translator from enforced literalness, and enlarging the translator's accountability to make the goal actually attained.

Read translated literature as a system within the target culture's social, literary, and historical systems, whose position is not fixed but shifts in a dynamic hierarchy between primary (innovatory, shaping the centre) and secondary (peripheral, conservative, and the normal position), occupying a primary position when a literature is young, peripheral or weak, or in crisis or vacuum.

Adopt a descriptive, target-organized, functional, and systemic view of literary translation with continual interplay between theoretical models and case studies, focused on the norms and constraints that govern the production and reception of translations.

Analyse translation as rewriting that projects an author's image beyond its culture, controlled by professionals inside the literary system who set the dominant poetics and by patronage outside it that sets the ideology through ideological, economic, and status components, and expect that when linguistic considerations conflict with ideological or poetological ones the latter win, so ideology and the dominant target poetics dictate the strategy.

Treat translated literature as a system with its own repertoire, not a random set of texts (its works correlate in how their source texts are selected — selection always tied to the target literature's home co-systems — and in the norms they adopt), and hold its position within the literary polysystem to be variable rather than fixed: central or peripheral, innovatory (primary) or conservatory (secondary), depending on the constellation under study.

Expect translated literature to assume a central, innovating position under three conditions (one law) — when a literature is young and being established, when it is peripheral or weak within a larger group, and at turning points, crises, or vacuums — where it introduces new models and blurs the line between original and translated writing; and expect it in the peripheral position to employ secondary models and become a major factor of conservatism, adhering to norms the centre has rejected, so that a vehicle for new ideas can ossify into a systeme d'antan (empirically the 'normal' position tends to be peripheral, and rigid systems keep it extremely so).

Locate translation within the literary system's two controls: patronage, the regulatory body with ideological, economic, and status components (usually exerted through critics, and either undifferentiated under one ideology or differentiated among competing ideologies), and poetics, the code with an inventory component (genres, symbols, characters, prototypical situations) and a functional component (how literature may function in society) that is singular under undifferentiated patronage but plural and stratified into 'high' and 'low' under differentiated patronage.

Let the position of translated literature condition the strategy: when it is primary, break target conventions and produce an adequate target text that reproduces the source's textual relations, and when it is secondary, use existing target-culture models and produce more acceptable, non-adequate translations.

Do descriptive translation studies with an explicit, systematic method so findings are intersubjectively testable, comparable, and replicable, treating translations first as facts of the target culture whose position determines strategy, and applying Toury's three-phase methodology of situating the text in the target system, analysing coupled source-target pairs to identify obligatory and non-obligatory shifts, and generalizing about the patterns to reconstruct the process, repeating across similar pairs.

Reconstruct the norms operating in a translation, which are the community's shared values turned into performance instructions, specific to a culture and time and sitting on a potency cline between rules and idiosyncrasies and graded in intensity, from the regularities in the texts and from explicit statements treated cautiously as possibly biased.

Treat being a translator as playing a socially allotted role whose prerequisite is acquiring the norms for what is suitable and for manoeuvring among competing constraints (not reducible to generating 'translation' utterances): those constraints lie on a scale between relatively absolute rules and purely individual idiosyncrasies, with the vast intersubjective middle occupied by norms (themselves a graded continuum that shift over time as whims become norms and norms harden into rules); norms translate a community's shared values into performance instructions specifying what is prescribed, forbidden, tolerated, and permitted, so — since there is no necessary identity between a norm and any verbal formulation of it, and stated norms are slanted by a desire to control — reconstruct the actual norms from regularities of behaviour rather than from what practitioners say they do.

Map the norms operating at each stage: the initial norm, the general choice between source norms giving an adequate translation and target-culture norms giving an acceptable one on a continuum; the preliminary norms of translation policy for text selection and directness of translation through an intermediate language; and the operational norms comprising matricial norms of completeness (omissions, relocations, segmentation, added passages or footnotes) and textual-linguistic norms of lexical and stylistic selection.

Use Toury's structure of translational norms: preliminary norms (with logical and chronological precedence) govern translation policy — the non-random set of factors determining which text-types and texts a culture imports at a given time — and directness, the tolerance for indirect translation through a mediating language (permitted, prohibited, tolerated, or preferred, and whether the mediation is marked, ignored, camouflaged, or denied); operational norms govern the act itself, subdividing into matricial norms (the existence, fullness, location, and segmentation of the target material, hence omissions, additions, and relocations) and textual-linguistic norms (the selection of the linguistic material).

Recognize that euphemistic or altered translations reveal a society's dominant ideology and, for readers who cannot read the source, become the text, and that rewriting before or during translation by omitting, softening, or altering sensitive passages is driven by ideological and commercial pressures.

Read theorists' own agendas critically and detect ideological manipulation in the target text, whether from the translator or from commissioner, editor, or institutional pressure and especially in news translation, using discourse, critical-discourse, and narrative analysis, while recognizing the macro forces of censorship, the epistemicide of English academic hegemony, and language imbalance, including informal translation in multilingual cities.

Read a translation's cuts and adaptations against its imagined audience and market, which systematically shape what is suppressed, and against the distance between the source and target audiences, which forces adaptation; and judge a translator not for cutting content but for concealing it — transparency about what is cut matters more than whether something is cut.

Locate the deep problem of translating a foreign work not in the dictionary or semantic equivalence but in a compromise between two poetics in which the receiving system's poetics dominates (translators of Brecht made explicit what he wanted the audience to piece together, added italics and stage directions, and padded songs into the Broadway-musical register), against which refractors of an alien poetics deploy four strategies — accepting the works while dismissing the poetics, psychologizing the poetics as rationalized temperament, assimilating it by translating its concepts into the old terminology, or explaining it and showing the system can accommodate it; therefore do not judge translations in isolation as simply good or bad, since a later source-faithful version can afford its fidelity only because earlier compromising translations first established a bridgehead and started the critical debate, expect no necessary progression toward a single definitive translation (language, politics, and the refracting spectrum keep shifting, and literary systems are stochastic), and account for the many changes explicable only by ideology rather than comprehension — playing down or omitting charged content, raising loaded words to a nobler register, and removing profanity to satisfy the receiving system's codes.

Do not translate from a position of monolingual superiority: the native's withholding (Friday's erased rebus in Coetzee's Foe, the transmission marked 'not a story to pass on' in Morrison's Beloved) figures the limit of translation, so untranslatability can be a marked and honored condition rather than a failure to be overcome by the confident accessibility of the powerful; the too-easy accessibility of translation as a transfer of substance reduces its object, so attend instead to the rhetoric that points to the limits of translation in a marginalized speaker's use of the dominant language, remembering that reading is itself a form of translation in which the post-colonial reader-as-translator reads a dominant text critically — using what is useful, discriminating on the terrain of the original, and noticing where the text swerves or keeps its argument domestic.

Understand committed and identity-based translation: feminist theory critiques the sexist metaphors of the field and directs fidelity to the shared writing project, a committed project openly manipulates the text as a political activity with visible strategies, and identity markers such as those of queer or camp discourse may disappear, be made pejorative, or be intensified according to target-culture attitudes and commercial pressures.

Explain a translation's minimization or amplification of a marked identity-discourse by the target culture's prevailing conception of human subjectivity: French Enlightenment universalism, suspicious of subcultural identity labels and of 'the temptation of the community', leads a French translator to suppress camp where Anglo-American identity politics would foreground it — so whether a marked discourse can accrue positive value in translation depends on the target polysystem's categories (where the identity category and an established minority literature are disabled, the associated register stays marginalized), and source categories such as French 'pederastic literature' must not be conflated with the target's understanding of 'gay literature'.

Contest value-free descriptions and account for the value-driven institutional network of a translation, including the publishers and editors who choose, commission, pay, and dictate method plus agents, marketing, and reviewers, and recognize the translator's invisibility in Anglo-American cultures produced both by fluent translation that creates an illusion of transparency and by readers judging a translation acceptable only when it reads as the original rather than a translation.

Investigate domesticating and foreignizing practices and the translator's invisibility by comparing source and target for tell-tale signs, interviewing translators and publishers, and examining translation volumes, trends, contracts, packaging visibility, and reviews, and take Berman's ethical aim of receiving the Foreign as Foreign, treating translation as a trial both for the target culture experiencing the foreign and for the uprooted source.

Screen a literary translation for Berman's twelve deforming tendencies (rationalization, clarification, expansion, ennoblement, qualitative and quantitative impoverishment, destruction of rhythms, of underlying networks of signification, of linguistic patternings, and of vernacular networks or their exoticization, destruction of expressions and idioms, and effacement of the superimposition of languages), refusing to replace a source idiom with a target equivalent or to seek a target vernacular for a source vernacular, and pursue instead a positive labour on the letter that attends to the work's signifying process.

Use Berman's twelve deforming tendencies as a systematic diagnostic that bears on all translating in the western tradition: rationalization, clarification, expansion, ennoblement and popularization, qualitative impoverishment, quantitative impoverishment, the destruction of rhythms, the destruction of underlying networks of signification, the destruction of linguistic patternings, the destruction of vernacular networks or their exoticization, the destruction of expressions and idioms, and the effacement of the superimposition of languages.

Study a translation's reception through reviews and paratexts, distinguishing peritexts (in the same volume, from author or publisher) from epitexts (freely circulating reviews, marketing, and criticism) that guide the reading, analysing reviews synchronically or diachronically against the readers' horizon of expectation, and expecting reviews to prefer fluent translations, rarely discuss the translation, and treat the translator's words as the author's own, confirming the translator's invisibility.

Critique a translation by analyzing its concrete textual features — lexicon, syntax, prosody, discourse — and explaining them through the translator's literary habits, the traditions of the translating language, and the cultural values and political interests those choices invest in, rather than by an abstract fidelity score.

Treat literary translation as an interpretive act proceeding through Steiner's hermeneutic motion of initiative trust, aggression, incorporation, and compensation, grounding faithfulness ethically in restoring the balance that appropriation disrupts, and recognizing that incorporation can enrich or infect the target culture and enhance or consume the translator and that great translation arises from an unresolved but expressive tension between resistant difference and elective affinity that is greater the closer the two cultures are.

Keep the ethics of the foreign in view: translating is at once sympathetic and violent, exploitive and ethically restorative (Steiner), so great translation must carry the most precise possible sense of the resistant — the barriers intact at the heart of understanding — rather than erase the text's difficulty, and beware that the maxim that a translation should not seem translated mystifies its own appropriation (Meschonnic), masking an annexation of the foreign under an illusion of transparency that, forgetting its history, risks imperialism.

Model translation as Steiner's fourfold hermeneutic motion — initiative trust, aggression, incorporation, and restitution — which supersedes the sterile triad of literalism, paraphrase, and free imitation and is inherent in even the rudiments of translation; its first move, trust, is an a priori leap that grants 'there is something there' to understand and that the transfer will not be void, a gamble on the world's coherence and symbolic plenitude that nonsense, glossolalia, and concrete poetry betray by being lexically non-communicative and hence untranslatable.

Where language deconstructs its own premises, as in philosophical or self-referential texts, apply Lewis's abusive fidelity, an experimental strategy that tampers with target usage to match the source's polyvalencies and bears upon a key operator while resisting domesticating use-values, recognizing that it fails when the source is flattened by typographical changes, dropped suffixes, lost precision, altered order, or unrecreated wordplay, and extend it to abusive subtitling.

Recognize that conventional translation of expository writing privileges the capture of signifieds — giving primacy to message and concept over language texture, so it works by substitution while losing the order of syntax and metonymy that carries the original's textual work — and adopt Lewis's new axiomatics of fidelity, which demands fidelity to far more than semantic substance (the chain of signifiers, syntactic processes, discursive structures, and rhetorical strategies) and shifts the translator's problem from avoiding inevitable failures to compensating for losses and renewing signifying energy; direct any abusive move not at just any element but at a key operator or decisive textual knot — a cluster of textual energy that resists the preponderant values of the usual and useful — since abusive translation foreignizes in two directions at once, forcing the target language from within and directing a critical thrust back at the source so that the original is rendered still more foreign to itself.

Treat film as multi-channel, multi-code communication (verbal, literary-theatrical, proxemic-kinetic, and cinematic) constrained by an inviolable image that must not be contradicted and a retained source soundtrack, treat interlingual subtitling as a diagonal translation that renders both source-to-target and speech-to-writing, and know the audiovisual types of interlingual and bilingual subtitling, intralingual subtitling for the hard of hearing, dubbing, voice-over, surtitling, and audio description.

Analyse an audiovisual text across its signifying codes (Chaume's ten, only one linguistic, four acoustic and six visual) and through multimodal transcription of frames, shots, and phases with a metafunctional interpretation, remembering that the linguistic code is written to be spoken as if not written and demands an oral register, that its problems are shared with other translation types, that visual and colour codes constrain choices so an unfamiliar symbol may need explanation and coherence with the image must be kept, and that subtitling is an overt, vulnerable translation open to a viewer's scrutiny while the subtitler is often uncredited.

Design translation research with clear question types (definition, data, descriptive, and cause-and-effect) and hypothesis types (interpretive, descriptive, explanatory, and predictive), tested empirically against translations, translation processes, or the extralinguistic context.

Design a translation-studies research project by defining a specific, motivated topic, setting scope (an MA works its own data within an existing framework while a PhD makes an original contribution), posing research questions or hypotheses, reviewing the literature to locate the study and identify gaps, choosing a methodology across product-oriented (discourse and corpus), process-oriented (keystroke logging, eye-tracking, think-aloud), participant-oriented (questionnaires and interviews), and context-oriented (case study) research with attention to ethics, and keeping to a realistic, manageable timeline.

Judge a translation theory as a complete account of function/goal, operations, and the relation between them (Kelly), and stay alert that the component a theory over-emphasizes tends to harden a merely descriptive typology into a prescriptive norm — so treat such distinctions as historically-situated heuristics, not timeless categories.

Treat most so-called general theories of translation with suspicion: theoretical translation studies aims ultimately at a highly formalized general theory but has so far produced mainly prolegomena, and many purported general theories are in fact partial while being simultaneously too inclusive (covering non-translations) and too exclusive (shutting out recognized translations); the real advances live in partial theories restricted by medium, area, rank, text type, time, or problem — often several at once — and a body of such partial theories must not be mistaken for a true general theory.

Never let a version's popularity or influence certify its accuracy: a translation's fidelity is always in doubt and varies across versions of the same text, and the equivalence achieved in practice is partial and selective (a chosen subset of the source's values), so the most widely read version can be the least faithful.

Do not assume the received translation is accurate merely because it is the one everyone reads: a flawed version can become the canonical, standard form through copyright lock-in, and every translation is historically indexed and ages as the target language and culture shift, so a version faithful in its own time can later read as dated with no one at fault.

Read a translation in relation to the rival versions it reacts to, not in isolation (translators define themselves against their predecessors, and 'to be different' becomes a rule the precursor imposes); and because each translator distorts the original in a characteristic direction, comparing several independent versions lets a reviewer triangulate the source and expose each translator's investments.

Treat literary translations as facts of the target system governed by the norms of a polysystem (Even-Zohar, Toury), occupying central or peripheral positions and performing innovative or conservatory functions, and therefore judge not a translation's 'adequacy' to the source — shifts always occur, and even pairing a source text with a translation already applies a target norm — but its 'acceptability' in the receiving culture at its historical moment; this target orientation, with Holmes's pure/applied disciplinary map, is what constituted translation studies as a discipline.

Situate the work within Holmes's constitution of translation studies as an empirical discipline with two Hempelian objectives — to describe the phenomena of translating and translations as they manifest in experience, and to establish general principles that explain and predict them — whose map divides pure translation studies into descriptive translation studies (closest to the empirical phenomena) and theoretical translation studies, alongside applied areas such as translator training.

Locate applied work within Holmes's four areas — translator training, translation aids (specialized lexicographical and terminological tools and translation-matching grammars, since ordinary dictionaries and contrastive grammars fall short of translators' needs), translation policy (advising society on what to translate and on the translator's role), and translation criticism (still often intuitive but improvable through contact with scholarship) — and treat the descriptive, theoretical, and applied branches as dialectically interdependent, since one cannot begin work in any branch without at least an intuitive theoretical hypothesis.

Read a translation through Toury's initial norm — the translator's basic choice between subjecting himself to the source text and its norms (pursuing an adequate translation, close to the source but liable to clash with target conventions) or to the target culture's norms (yielding acceptability at the price of shifts from the source), a priority that is logical and explanatory, not chronological — and treat shifts from the source as a true universal of translation that occur even in the most adequacy-oriented work, where both the obligatory shifts and the more frequent non-obligatory ones are norm-governed rather than idiosyncratic.

Never assume a translated text is representative of the target language or of any overall textual tradition thereof, because translational norms may differ from the norms governing non-translational text production and their identity must not be taken for granted; and take Toury's central thesis that norms determine the type and extent of equivalence a translation manifests, which turns equivalence from an ahistorical, prescriptive concept into a historical one — not a single invariant relation but any relation found to characterize translation under a specified set of circumstances.

Accept that because no two languages are identical in their symbols or arrangements there can be no absolute correspondence and hence no fully exact translation — the total impact may be close but there is no identity in detail — so translation always involves interpretation and remains the most direct form of commentary.

Accept that a good translation faces a contradictory demand and is therefore always already a double interpretation — it must be faithful both to the language and message of the original and to the message-orienting cast of its own language, two mutually exclusive interpretations that consign every translation to a degree of inadequacy — and note that a translator who is also the author of the original can shift at will between conventional translation and compensating commentary, so that for the ordinary translator, deprived of the commentarial option, the central question is whether and how anything can be done to preserve the tenor, texture, and tangents the target language would otherwise override.

Reconstruct norms rather than read them off, because norms are not directly observable — what is available is norm-governed behaviour and most often only its products (even thinking-aloud protocols yield products) — drawing on two sources with their proper weight: textual sources (the translated texts themselves, primary products of norm-regulated behaviour) and extratextual sources (prescriptive theories and statements by translators, editors, and critics, which are mere partial, persuasion-biased by-products never to be accepted at face value but explicated and confronted with the patterns of actual behaviour).
Treat textual products as primary evidence for norms and extratextual formulations as secondary interpretive evidence that must be controlled.

Recognize the relative autonomy of the translated text as the most common assumption of 1980s theory: across semiotic, discourse-analytic, and poststructuralist approaches, translation is treated as an independent form of writing distinct from the foreign text and from texts originally written in the translating language and enacting its own processes of signification — Frawley's 'third code' rejecting equivalence as identity on the ground that 'there is information only in difference' (a translation is a code in its own right, setting its own standards while remaining derivative of source information and target parameters), and Blum-Kulka's explicitation hypothesis holding that translation tends always to increase the semantic relations and cohesion of a text through explicitness, repetition, redundancy, and explanation, a translating-specific discourse type later confirmed by corpus study.

Follow Frawley's argument that a respectable theory of translation must abandon the notions of good, bad, and fidelity just as it abandoned identity and 'preservation of meaning' — since strict fidelity to the source produces awkward rather than interesting texts and would make machines the best translators — and can at most classify a translation as a moderate innovation (a close translation adhering to the matrix or a free translation adhering to the target, both yielding only moderate new information) or a radical innovation that breaks from both codes and carries the most semiotic information, because translation is an act of sign-production, not sign-translation: the new code is a semiotic unit that signifies by its own individuation rather than a universal significance disembodied and reincarnated.

Hold in view the manipulation and poststructuralist reconception of translation: for the manipulation school translation is never an untroubled communication of a foreign text but a manipulation shaped by patronage, poetics, and ideology, while poststructuralism reconceives language as a site of uncontrollable polysemy and translation as interrogative or deconstructive (Derrida), reducing source meanings while releasing target potentialities that redound unsettlingly on the foreign text, and thereby reviving untranslatability more corrosively than Quine by locating the problem in the inherent indeterminacy of language — in irreducible differences not only between languages and cultures but within them.

Reckon with untranslatability rather than defensively dismiss it — texts whose strategy leaves relations indeterminate through operators of undecidability (as in Derrida) are exceptionally resistant, and because the combinations of use and abuse are elusive and impracticable to program, translation is essayistic in the strong sense, emerging in an experimental order of discovery where success depends on trial, error, and chance as well as on language's paraphrastic capacities — and evaluate an abusive-fidelity translation by three moves applied through close line-by-line and word-by-word comparison: concentrate on the moments of density and intensity where the play of concepts is affected by the disruptive power of language, insist on the transformations the translation makes at the syntactic and discursive levels and not just the semantic, and ask whether the translation articulates its own textual effects that are tellingly abusive with respect to the original.

Ground a translation ethics in Berman's 'trial of the foreign': bad translation is ethnocentric and mystifying, performing under the cloak of transmissibility a systematic negation of the foreignness of the foreign work through largely unconscious deforming tendencies, whereas good translation respects the foreign differences through a correspondence that enlarges, amplifies, and enriches the translating language.

Frame translation, with Berman, as the trial of the foreign in a double sense: it establishes a relation between the Self-Same and the Foreign by aiming to open the foreign work to us in its utter foreignness (which classic translations tend to attenuate or cancel), and it is a trial for the Foreign as well, since the work is uprooted from its language-ground in an exile that can reveal its most deeply buried kernel — so that (with Hollderlin) translating means liberating the violence repressed in a work through intensifications that accentuate its strangeness, paradoxically the only way to give the reader genuine access.

Understand that an ethics which would preserve the foreignness of the foreign text can only be practiced in domestic terms — the foreign's differences signalled indirectly by their displacement into a domestic difference introduced at home — which makes such an ethics simultaneously a political agenda that disarranges the target culture's ranking of values to set going defamiliarization, canon reformation, ideological critique, and institutional change; and recognize that there is no true invariant transmitted in translation, since the source message is always interpreted and reinvented according to the target's values and variable across languages and moments, so the very need to 'establish the invariant' shows that translating does something more and other than communicate, and the descriptive turn that studies a translation's acceptability against domestic norms sidesteps the foreign rather than solving it.

Attend to the ideological asymmetries that structure translation: a patriarchal model of authority expressed through gender metaphors recurring since the seventeenth century has underwritten translation's subordinate status (so a feminist attention to gender can recover forgotten translating women and inform translation sensitive to ideologically coded writing), and a postcolonial reflection reveals translation as an agent or subverter of empire, since asymmetrical pressures between the languages of dominant and dominated societies structure the representation of the foreign and can vitiate the ethnographic 'cultural translation' enterprise.

Recognize translation figured as colonization and conquest — a strategy of linguistic incorporation enriching the language of expanding nations (the German Romantics used ubersetzen and verdeutschen interchangeably, and for the Romans translation was a form of conquest), cast repeatedly in imagery of sexual and colonial violence — and that the meaning of 'fidelity' is therefore not stable but flexes with the ideology it serves, defining either the female translation's regulated relation to the male original or the male translator's relation to his female mother tongue, in the latter guise even justifying the pillage of another language, since both versions ultimately certify the translation's originality and enrich the host language.

Ground a feminist practice of translation in the double bind rather than the double standard, replacing the oedipal family model of struggle with a model of collaboration that is at once cooperative and subversive: faced with an ideologically offensive source the resisting translator subverts the text — playing infidelity against infidelity and following out its parodic logic rather than declining to translate it, since refusal would capitulate to the very logic that ascribes all power to the original — and gives voice rather than silence by becoming an independent interpreter who speaks with the work and makes the principles of the practice explicit (so that writing about a translation matters as much as the translation itself), the decisive target being not the sex of the author or translator but the process by which translation complies with gender constructs.

Do not treat translation as a catalogue of 'howlers' — which leads only to damning all translation or demanding ever 'better' translators — but study constructively how translations actually mediate a work into another culture, accepting misunderstanding as a fact of literature, because a writer's exposure and influence come mainly through refractions: audiences reach an author through an image created from misunderstandings and misconceptions, refracted through a certain spectrum, rather than through direct osmosis of genius.

Treat translation, criticism, editing, and historiography as forms of refraction or rewriting that carry a work from one literary system into another and thereby establish a writer's reputation and, through anthologies and formal education, conservatively determine which works are canonized — an analysis that gives literary translation the seriousness usually reserved for original composition and exposes the Romantic assumptions unable to admit refraction: the ex-nihilo genius, the sacred untouchable text (hence the horror at 'bad' translations), the recoverability of the author's true intentions, and the judging of works on intrinsic merit alone.

Understand that coherence, as the realization of a text's meaning potential, shifts in two ways under translation — text-focused shifts linked to the translation process and reader-focused shifts linked to the change of audience, the reader-focused ones being the less avoidable — because coherence is reader- and schema-dependent (a text coheres only when the reader can apply relevant world, subject, and genre schemas, so King Lear does not mean the same to a British reader as to a French one); and since a target audience is almost always new to part of the source writer's shared world yet the prevailing modern norm treats a translation as rendering a given text rather than conveying a message to a new audience, reader-focused shifts are largely unavoidable unless the translator is normatively free to transplant the text into another cultural environment.

Beware that over-clarifying a culture-specific detail to help the target reader can destroy the indirect, figurative meaning it carries across a text (Pinter's Hebrew translator spelling out a casserole's ingredients lost the running metaphor that carries the play's marital-triangle subtext), and recognize that translation reverses the residual ambiguity of natural conversation — what is said becoming obvious while what is meant becomes vague; study cohesion shifts validly by separating obligatory choices dictated by the two grammars from optional stylistic ones, since only optional shifts are evidence of a translation trend, and study translation as a process that operates on texts rather than words or sentences (so that its products belong to discourse analysis) and as an act of communication whose processes, products, and effects must be validated empirically, ideally by psycholinguistic comparison of how source-language and target-language readers actually interpret the text.

Recognize that the opposition between productive and reproductive work codes originality as paternity and authority — marking writing as original and 'masculine' and translating as derivative and 'feminine' — and that this is only superficially aesthetic, carrying real consequences in publishing, royalties, curriculum, and tenure, since translation is culturally coded as the artificial, false, and treasonous copy set against a natural, truthful, lawful original, a coding institutionalized in copyright law's treatment of translations as 'derivative works'.

Understand that this metaphorics encodes the relation between the value of production and reproduction with power consistently at stake: fidelity regulates paternity and hence property and legitimacy (a translation of non-public-domain work legally requires the author's consent), and translation is so heavily over-regulated precisely because it threatens to erase the production/reproduction boundary by masquerading as an original — a danger figured as the original's death or emasculation — even as translation is materially subordinated despite the academy's heavy reliance on it, with reviews omitting the translator, projects deemed marginal for tenure, and even the best translators poorly paid.

Analyze whole actual translations across style, genre, discourse, pragmatics, and ideology (Hatim and Mason), transcending the literary/non-literary split, and apply politeness theory (where 'face' is the want to be unimpeded and approved of) to expose losses such as film subtitling systematically shedding, under its temporal and spatial constraints, the politeness phenomena by which characters accommodate each other's face-wants; and use corpus study to seek features distinctive of translation itself — explicitation, normalization, lexical density, and sanitization — while remembering that computerized, globally-governed analysis tends to emphasize norms over innovative strategies and to describe production to the exclusion of reception.

Weight the seriousness of a face-threatening act as a cultural variable set by the social distance and relative power of the speakers (a direct request is less threatening among friends than across a hierarchy, and pronouns of address are a site of complex face-negotiation), remembering that although the underlying strategies of politeness are remarkably uniform across cultures their linguistic realization varies, so politeness can be relayed trans-culturally but requires modification at the level of texture; and recognize that film dialogue is doubly designed — characters address each other within the fiction while the scriptwriter constructs the dialogue for the mass audience as auditors who are often more important than the immediate addressees — so the subtitler must relay both a character's on-screen discourse and the scriptwriter's signal to the audience.

Treat translation as identity-forming and politically inscriptive: it creates representations of foreign texts that answer to the interests of the translating culture and are determined by ethnicity, gender, class, and nation, so strongly ethnocentric translating has underwritten imperialism (rendering Native American kinship into the European identity of property, or inscribing colonial translations with a stereotype that rationalized British domination in India), and although translation can be turned to forge a national cultural identity (Quebecois translators raising their French through world dramatists), a struggle against one linguistic hierarchy can install another, since versions that reduce the foreign's differences cultivate a homogeneous sameness in which doing away with any ambiguity of identity means getting rid of the Other.

Recognize that translating identity-marked discourse such as 'camp' is target-culture-dependent (a French translator omitted the camp of an American gay novel while an American translator amplified it) and that a tool-kit approach, using whatever analytical concept proves useful, shows universalizing linguistic models such as politeness theory's rational, face-protecting 'Model Person' must be revised for specific communities; and take Venuti's argument that prevailing fluent strategies produce an illusion of transparency that lets a translation pass for the original and renders the translator invisible — masking an appropriative, potentially imperialistic domestication that extends the global hegemony of English — which can be countered by a foreignizing, experimentalist translation that registers the foreign text's irreducible differences, though only in domestic terms by deviating from currently dominant target values, so that the ethical choice is between sameness (ethnocentric translating that smooths institutions) and difference (ethnodeviant translating that prizes innovation to stimulate institutional change), an ethics of location whose valuation shifts with the translating culture's position in local, national, and global hierarchies.

Understand that when a culture's referential language is a foreign one felt to be alienating, translation becomes a re-territorializing operation that does not create a new language but supplants the Other's with a native vernacular, elevating a dialect to national and cultural status as an act of reclaiming identity; that marking the target language of a translation ('traduit en quebecois') reverses the usual practice of naming only the source and is thus an ideological act underscoring the language's marginality and constructing a distinct identity; and that translation can be turned to the target's self-legitimation rather than to mediating a foreign work, so that rendering canonical masterpieces into a dialect reverses the roles and gives the foreign work the mission of vouching for the existence of the translating language and its 'people', becoming that community's mirror.

Accept that translation never communicates in an untroubled fashion, because it inscribes the foreign text with a domestic significance: the translator negotiates the source's linguistic and cultural differences by reducing them and supplying another, basically domestic, set of differences drawn from the receiving culture, so the foreign is not so much communicated as inscribed with domestic intelligibilities and interests — a totalizing though never total inscription that begins with the selective, densely motivated choice of a text to translate, continues in the choice of certain domestic discourses over others, and operates in every word before readers even further process it.

Preserve, with Spivak, the rhetoricity of the language of Third World literatures (rhetoric's disruption of logic and grammar), because rendering such works into an immediately accessible 'with-it translatese' strips them of their linguistic, cultural, and geopolitical differences and enacts a neocolonialist construction of the non-Western scene — favouring a literalist 'in-between discourse' that gives a tough sense of the original's terrain, while heeding her warning that political valence is contingent, so what seems resistant in English may be reactionary in the original; and consider Appiah's 'thick translation', which uses annotations and glosses to locate a text in a rich cultural context on the view that a literary translation creates a relationship to the target conventions matching the foreign text's relationship to its own culture — a match that may be unfaithful to literal intentions in order to preserve formal features, and whose value is ultimately settled in pedagogy.

Treat translation as the most intimate act of reading, requiring the translator to surrender to the text — overcoming the schoolroom prize for the most accurate string of synonyms in the closest syntax and resisting both the solemnity of ornate poetic prose and the forced simplicity of 'plain English' — and to construct a model of how the other language stages agency through a three-part structure of rhetoric, logic, and silence (logic jumping from word to word by clear connections while rhetoric works in the silence between and around words), a different effort from treating translation as a matter of synonym, syntax, and local colour, because without a sense of rhetoricity a neo-colonialist construction of the non-Western scene is afoot that no argument for convenience can justify.

Recognize that a translation can amplify a marked discourse rather than merely render it, adding un-source-based material that reframes the whole scene and attributing agency that transforms its meaning (turning a child's role-play into homosexual seduction) under a systematic transformation driven by the target culture's social movement and publisher rather than neutral equivalence — and therefore relate the minutiae of textual analysis to the interactional, social, and political contexts that produce and are acted on by language forms, since translation is about the relation of the one to the other, giving that relationship between setting and discourse the force of causality while avoiding both context-blind text-linguistics and text-thin appeals to power.

Recognize that a colonial writer's or translator's dilemma is sharpened by diglossia rather than bilingualism — the distance between an indigenous spoken language and a foreign written one that share the same heritage — and that populist rhetoric urging writers to 'give the power of speech back to the people' can mask an elite institutional reappropriation, since the writers do not themselves speak that language and the demand really serves to prove a group's absolute difference and secure institutional recognition; apply instead Luther's grassroots principle of observing how ordinary people actually speak (seeking the mother at home, the children in the streets, the common man in the marketplace), because the success of a translation and of any institution built on it depends on a real public recognizing its own speech, and note that a language shared with a rival culture can be deliberately re-defined as 'foreign' to assert its illegitimacy, with the chosen genre staging that difference (theatre's primacy of the oral making the phonetic difference between a referential and a vernacular form audible).

Read the surrounding diglossia as evidence of a translation's ideological rather than mediating function: in a theatre system that has raised the vernacular to literary status the 'naturalist' code becomes the equivalent of the older literary code, so a claimed irreconcilable difference between the two languages is often minimal in the actual text (Tremblay's Uncle Vanya carries the marked sociolect only in one servant's speech), and translators who render the foreign text in the vernacular but explain it in the standard-language preface, stage directions, and commentary thereby introduce an ideology to a public from which they exclude themselves — so that rejecting a long-understood translation as suddenly 'inaccessible', such that the reader must detour through a third language, is ideology masquerading as a comprehension need, in a climate where the translator's nationality becomes a criterion for legitimizing the work.

Let the principle of relevance constrain both what a translation conveys (only the respects that make it adequately relevant to the receptor, yielding adequate contextual effects) and how it is expressed (so as to yield the intended interpretation without unnecessary processing effort), remembering that a rendering can fail on two counts at once — a mismatch in a word's associated encyclopaedic and connotative information and an increase in processing cost (choosing 'thou' for French 'tu' to preserve intimacy but reading as obsolete or ecclesiastical, its rare form making readers expect a payoff and reach for unintended implications) — because a reader takes not the first interpretation that comes to mind but the first that both comes to mind and is consistent with relevance, so a costly, opaque rendering that yields no significant contextual implications forces the reader to invest extra effort at the risk of misreading, to assume the translation is faulty, or to discard it.

Do not treat a feature's high relevance in the original as sufficient for its inclusion, nor let preserving a text's abstract features license discarding its concrete ones — four alternative renderings that lose that the animal was a weasel are less faithful than they could reasonably have been, since that identifying resemblance could have been kept at no extra processing cost — and reckon with a resemblance/effort trade-off in which a higher degree of resemblance is sometimes achievable only at a decrease in overall relevance (demanding processing effort not outweighed by contextual effects), so that under those conditions the less-resembling rendering is the one required; a relevance account accordingly does not predict that all translation succeeds, but predicts that failure is likely precisely where the translator's assumptions about the receptor audience's cognitive environment are inaccurate.

Aim to communicate to domestic readers the understanding that foreign readers have, while accepting that this is only partial — always incomplete and slanted toward the domestic scene, and achievable only when the domestic remainder the translation releases includes an inscription of the foreign context in which the text first emerged — a second-order communication that is built upon but signifies beyond lexicographical equivalence and exceeds mere information, conveying an interpretation that participates in the work's afterlife and is shared by the source's own readers, thereby partly restoring the foreign text's historical context, though for domestic readers.

Recognize that the domestic inscription creates a heterogeneous domestic community of interest around a translated text — an audience to whom it is intelligible and who put it to varied uses — so that a translation is a linguistic zone of contact not only between the foreign and translating cultures but within the translating culture, which it decenters across lines of social differentiation, becoming a site of interpretive communities that may support or challenge prevailing canons, standards, and ideologies and, because it traffics in the foreign, may either cross or reinforce the boundaries and hierarchies between domestic audiences (a canonical text's translation forming an interpretive-community battleground, a mass-circulation text's fostering unexpected groupings of readers otherwise separated by cultural difference).

Note that a single translation can appeal simultaneously to multiple incommensurable communities through a mixed register (Mandelbaum's Ungaretti adhered to the terse fragmentation prized by the Italian academic readership while introducing a strain of Victorian poeticism that addressed a different domestic readership), and that a translation's standard of accuracy typically embodies the prevailing interpretation of a particular interpretive community — Mandelbaum's strict lexicographical equivalence enacted the reading favored by Italian academic specialists, whose esteem an appeal to 'universal' value actually named only a professional and potential, not a genuinely universal, community.

Recognize that translating a foreign work into the dominant translation discourse of the target culture is a canonizing gesture that can invert the source's actual significance (Mandelbaum rendered Ungaretti's spare, ornament-purging modernism in the ornate Victorian poeticism favored by 1950s American poetry translators, and, as with Lattimore and Ciardi, his stated norm of plainness contradicted his actual archaizing practice), and that a domesticating remainder is invisible to those lacking either target-literary competence or source knowledge — American reviewers commented on the translation as if it were the Italian, and the Italian academics did not register the Victorian poeticism — so that only a doubly-competent reader, a native reader of the target poetry who also knows the source text and its tradition, can perceive it.

Understand that to translate is to invent for a foreign text new readerships and an imagined community, in Anderson's sense — members who never meet yet share an image of their communion derived from the representation the translator has domestically inscribed, shared even among readers whose interests are incommensurable — and that a translated bestseller, to reach a mass audience assembled from the most diverse domestic constituencies, must widen the domestic appeal at the cost of the foreign context, risking the reduction of the foreign text to what those constituencies have in common, its reception then varying by each constituency's values (Bonjour Tristesse read in Anglo-America through post-war moral panic rather than as an accomplished work of art).

Recognize that free, fluent translation produces the illusion of transparency that lets the reader take the translation for the foreign text (reviewers praised a translator's prose as if it were the author's), while the same freedoms inscribe the target culture's values through small additions (inserting 'secret' into 'a secret desire for her' makes the narrative speak to a morality that would conceal sexuality, an odd effect in a novel about an unconcealed one), so that translating is at once ideological and utopian — an asymmetrical act of communication weighted toward the translating culture, releasing a domestic remainder that inscribes domestic values and provides an ideological resolution of the foreign text's differences, yet made with the very intention to communicate the foreign and so projecting a hoped-for, not-yet-realized community gathered around that text.
